newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia minister rejects call for U.N. force.
newsitem.headline: Colombia minister rejects call for U.N. force.

text.p: Colombia's defence minister on Tuesday rejected a call by the governor of one of the country's most violent provinces for U.N. peace-keeping troops to be drafted into the area to safeguard human rights.

Defence Minister Guillermo Alberto Gonzalez quickly turned down the suggestion by Gov. Alvaro Uribe, who had said an international force should be deployed in the trouble-torn, banana-growing region of Uraba, part of northwest Antioquia province near the border with Panama.
Leftist guerrillas and right-wing death squads have killed with impunity for more than a decade in the area.

In the latest incident there, investigators said they had unearthed five corpses in shallow graves near the town of Apartado, which was also the site of a car bomb attack last week in which 11 people died.

"A request from Colombia for armed support from the UN... would reaffirm our sovereignty and show the international community this is a respectable state that wishes to regain respect for human rights," Uribe told reporters after a meeting in the provincial capital, Medellin.

Gonzalez rejected the plan in comments to the press in Bogota, saying: "That's just not possible. The presence of blue berets is not applicable to these types of internal conflicts like that in Uraba."

President Ernesto Samper and army commanders, not wanting to give an international dimension to Colombia's three-decade-old guerrilla uprising, have also ruled out all offers of assistance from foreign leaders to mediate with Marxist rebels.

Uribe's critics blame him for fuelling the violence through covert backing of right-wing paramilitary groups and his open sponsorship of anti-guerrilla civilian self-defence committees, known as Convivirs.
International human rights groups have criticised the Convivirs, whose members have the right to bear weapons, as little more than legalised death squads.
The discovery of the five dead men near Apartado appeared to demonstrate the unstoppable spiral of tit-for-tat violence.

Local officials said the victims from the village of San Jose -- known locally as a hotbed of rebel support -- were probably killed by paramilitaries in revenge for last Thursday's bomb attack, which was blamed on guerrillas.
